pos: n. (Richard Furman, 1755–1825, pastor at Charleston, first president of the Triennial Convention)
etymology: Old German Ricohard, strong in rule; Furman, from German Fuhrmann, a carter.
biblical_def: Richard Furman was converted as a boy under Separate Baptist preaching in the South Carolina back country, began to preach at sixteen, and from 1787 to his death was pastor of the First Baptist Church of Charleston, the most influential Baptist pulpit in the South. He was the chief architect of Baptist cooperation in America: president of the Triennial Convention from its founding in 1814, the first body to unite Baptists nationally for foreign missions, and the driving force behind the South Carolina state convention of 1821, the pattern for every state convention since. He pressed relentlessly for an educated ministry, arguing that Baptists had suffered for want of it, and the college that became Furman University grew from his plans. He also, in 1822, wrote an exposition defending slaveholding from Scripture, addressed to the governor of South Carolina — a document that must be named plainly as a grave misuse of the Bible by a man who otherwise served it well. “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) was his principle for the ministry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a convention as an assembly of delegates, and a seminary as a place of education.
webster_full: CONVEN'TION, n. An assembly of delegates or representatives for consultation.
SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university.
ASSOCIA'TION, n. A society of persons united for a common purpose; a confederacy.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
corruption_summary: Charleston's pastor and architect of Baptist cooperation — and a defender of slavery.
corruption_paragraphs: Furman's 1822 Exposition of the Views of the Baptists argued that the holding of slaves is not condemned by Scripture, and it was influential. It was wrong, and it was wrong by the very method he claimed to use: the law he appealed to makes man-stealing a capital crime (Exo 21:16), and the trade that supplied his state was man-stealing. A man may serve the church ably for forty years and still put his learning at the disposal of an evil his neighbours profited by.

The principle to recover is that the use of Scripture is not validated by the piety of the user. Furman's own rule for the ministry — commit it “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — includes the duty of those taught to test what they are handed, and the Southern Baptist bodies he built spent a century and a half undoing this part of his legacy.
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit, entrust; baptizo (G907), to baptize; matheteuo (G3100), to make disciples.
roots_lines: Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to teach, make disciples; Matthew 28:19.
usage: “commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — his case for an educated ministry.
“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) — the Triennial Convention, 1814.
“buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4) — the Baptist ordinance he defended.

pos: n. (Oliver Hart, 1723–1795, pastor at Charleston, founder of the Charleston Association)
etymology: Latin oliva, an olive tree; Hart, a surname from the stag.
biblical_def: Oliver Hart was a Pennsylvania carpenter who came to Charleston in 1749, the week after its only Baptist pastor died, and stayed thirty years. In 1751 he gathered the Charleston Association, the second Baptist association in America and the model for Baptist cooperation in the South: congregations wholly independent in government, voluntarily associated for counsel, for the examination and education of ministers, and for shared relief. He drew up its Summary of Church Discipline, raised a fund for the training of ministers, and travelled constantly among the back-country churches, where he worked to reconcile the orderly Regular Baptists of the coast with the fervent Separate Baptists of the interior — a reconciliation that eventually made the Southern Baptists one people. Driven out by the British in 1780, he spent his last years at Hopewell in New Jersey. The association rested on a plain argument from the nature of counsel: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an association as a society of persons united for a common purpose, and discipline as instruction and government.
webster_full: ASSOCIA'TION, n. A society of persons united for a common object; union; connection.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to laws and rules.
COUN'SEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request.
scriptures: Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works:
corruption_summary: Charleston's carpenter-pastor, who founded the association model for Southern Baptists.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The association answers the standing objection that congregational independence must mean isolation, and the opposite objection that cooperation must mean hierarchy. Hart's churches surrendered no authority whatever and still shared a ministerial fund, an examination process and a discipline manual. The arrangement is voluntary and therefore fragile, and it has worked for two and a half centuries.

The principle to recover is that counsel is a means God provides and independence does not abolish: “Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9); “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3); and the churches are to “consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works” (Heb 10:24), which requires that they know one another.
roots_summary: Hebrew shenayim (H8147), two; sakar (H7939), reward, wages; Greek paroxusmos from paroxusmos (G3948), a provoking.
roots_lines: Greek paroxusmos (G3948) — a stirring up, provocation; Hebrews 10:24.
usage: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9) — the Charleston Association, 1751.
“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — Regulars and Separates reconciled.
“consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works” (Heb 10:24) — associated but independent.

pos: n. (Morgan Edwards, 1722–1795, Welsh-born pastor at Philadelphia, the first historian of American Baptists)
etymology: Welsh Morgan, sea-born or sea-bright; Edwards, son of Edward.
biblical_def: Morgan Edwards was born in Monmouthshire, trained at Bristol Baptist College, served in Ireland, and from 1761 was pastor of the First Baptist Church of Philadelphia. His great service was antiquarian. From 1770 he travelled through the colonies on horseback gathering the records of every Baptist congregation he could reach — dates of constitution, names of ministers, numbers of members, local histories taken from the oldest surviving people — and published the Materials towards a History of the American Baptists, of which volumes on Pennsylvania and New Jersey appeared and the rest survive in manuscript. Without his notebooks the first century of Baptist life in the middle and southern colonies would be largely lost. He was also a founder of what became Brown University and a Loyalist in the Revolution, which cost him his standing. He knew what he was doing and why: “This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD” (Psa 102:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines materials as the substance of which anything is made, and an antiquary as one who studies and collects the remains of former ages.
webster_full: MATE'RIALS, n. The substance or matter of which anything is composed; collections for a work.
AN'TIQUARY, n. One versed in antiquity; one who studies and collects the remains of ancient times.
AN'NALS, n. A history of events in the order of time.
scriptures: This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Pro 10:7
The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
corruption_summary: The Philadelphia pastor whose notebooks preserved the first century of American Baptist life.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Edwards is a reminder that most of what a church remembers about itself was gathered by somebody who rode out to ask. He took down the recollections of old members in their eighties who had seen the founding of congregations in the 1690s, and no other record of those conversations exists.

The principle to recover is that such gathering is a duty, not a hobby: what God has done is to be “written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18), and a people who “will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) must first have the account in hand. The works of faithful men follow them (Rev 14:13) only if somebody writes them down.
roots_summary: Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write; dor (H1755), a generation; zeker (H2143), remembrance.
roots_lines: Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, inscribe, record; Psalm 102:18.
Hebrew dor (H1755) — a generation, an age; Psalm 102:18.
usage: “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18) — the Materials, from 1770.
“We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — records taken from the oldest members.
“their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13) — if somebody rides out and asks.

pos: n. (Daniel Marshall, 1706–1784, Separate Baptist pioneer, founder of the first Baptist church in Georgia)
etymology: Hebrew Daniyyel, God is my judge; Marshall, from Old French mareschal, a horse-servant, an officer.
biblical_def: Daniel Marshall was a Connecticut Congregationalist, awakened under Whitefield, who at about forty sold his farm and went as a missionary to the Mohawk Indians on the Susquehanna, and was driven out by the French and Indian War. He became a Baptist by conviction about 1754, was ordained among the Separate Baptists, and spent the next thirty years planting churches through Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. He was brother-in-law to Shubal Stearns and with him part of the Sandy Creek movement that carried the Separate Baptist awakening through the southern back country. In 1771 he crossed into Georgia, where Baptist preaching was illegal; he was arrested while praying at a service on Kiokee Creek, and the constable's wife was converted by what she heard at his trial. In 1772 he constituted the Kiokee church, the first Baptist congregation in Georgia. He could barely read and was an indefatigable preacher. “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion, and to itinerate as to travel from place to place.
webster_full: MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; a person sent to preach the gospel.
ITIN'ERATE, v.i. To travel from place to place, particularly for the purpose of preaching.
CONSTABLE, n. An officer of the peace; a civil officer with power to arrest.
scriptures: Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Luk 10:2
Therefore said he unto them, The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few: pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: The Separate Baptist pioneer arrested for praying in Georgia, who planted its first church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Marshall is a standing difficulty for every argument that a ministry requires formal qualification before it may be exercised. He was barely literate, began at forty, changed denomination in middle life, and planted churches across four colonies. He is also a standing difficulty for the opposite argument, since the movement he served spent its next generation acquiring exactly the education he lacked, and was right to.

The principle to recover is that the errand is to go: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15), with the labourers always fewer than the harvest requires (Luk 10:2). Being arrested at prayer is one of the ordinary forms of being “instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).
roots_summary: Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad; kerusso (G2784), to proclaim; therismos (G2326), harvest.
roots_lines: Greek ekballo (G1544) — to send forth, thrust out; Luke 10:2.
Greek ephistemi (G2186) — to stand by, be instant; 2 Timothy 4:2.
usage: “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — Virginia to Georgia.
“Go ye into all the world” (Mar 16:15) — at forty, with a sold farm.
“be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — arrested at prayer on Kiokee Creek.

pos: n. (Crawford Howell Toy, 1836–1919, Southern Seminary professor who resigned in 1879 over higher criticism)
etymology: Crawford, from the Scottish place-name, the ford of the crow; Toy, an English surname of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Crawford Howell Toy was professor of Old Testament at the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary at Greenville and then Louisville from 1869. He had studied at Berlin, absorbed the documentary criticism of the Pentateuch then dominant in German universities, and came to hold that the Mosaic books were composite and late, that the prophets did not predict Christ in the sense the New Testament asserts, and that the apostles' use of the Old Testament was accommodation rather than exegesis. When the implications became plain he offered his resignation, and in 1879 the trustees accepted it; James P. Boyce, the seminary's founder, who loved him, is said to have told him on the journey away that he would give his right arm to have him back believing. Toy went to Harvard as professor of Hebrew and abandoned orthodox Christianity. His case is the first great American seminary test of the question, and it was settled in the right direction, at real cost to real friendships. “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines criticism as the art of judging with propriety of a literary performance, and inspiration as the infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit.
webster_full: CRIT'ICISM, n. The art of judging with propriety concerning any object; a critical examination.
INSPIRA'TION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit; the conveying into the minds of men ideas by extraordinary influence.
RESIGNA'TION, n. The act of resigning or giving up, as a claim, possession or office.
scriptures: If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: The Southern Seminary professor whose 1879 resignation set the American terms of the question.
corruption_paragraphs: Toy's position is the ancestor of every subsequent accommodation: that the critical conclusions about the composition of the Old Testament may be accepted whole, and the doctrine of inspiration then adjusted to fit, usually by locating inspiration in the religious experience of the writers rather than in the text. Toy went further than most of his successors and admitted where it led, which is why his case is clarifying.

The principle to recover is the one our Lord asserts in passing, as a thing not in dispute: “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35). Prophecy “came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21), and every claim about the text is tested by the text (Isa 8:20) — not the reverse.
roots_summary: Greek luo (G3089), to loose, break; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed; phero (G5342), to be moved, borne along.
roots_lines: Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, dissolve, break; John 10:35.
Greek graphe (G1124) — a writing, the Scripture; John 10:35.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, move; 2 Peter 1:21.
usage: “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35) — the point at issue in 1879.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — what the trustees would not adjust.
“holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — against accommodation.

pos: n. (the Adopting Act, 1729, by which the Synod of Philadelphia adopted the Westminster standards)
etymology: Latin adoptare, to choose for oneself, to take to oneself.
biblical_def: The Adopting Act was passed by the Synod of Philadelphia in September 1729 and is the founding constitutional document of American Presbyterianism. The synod declared the Westminster Confession and Catechisms to be in all the essential and necessary articles good forms of sound words and systems of Christian doctrine, and required every minister and licentiate to subscribe them; but it provided that a candidate who scrupled at any article should state his scruple to the presbytery or synod, which would judge whether the point was essential and necessary, and if not, admit him. It thus did two things at once: it bound the church to a confession and it declined to make every clause of it a term of office. The arrangement has been read in opposite directions ever since — as strict subscription with a narrow allowance, or as loose subscription with a confessional preface — and the argument has split American Presbyterians more than once. What the synod would not do was leave the question open. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to adopt as to take a stranger as one's own, to receive as one's own; and essential as necessary to the existence of a thing.
webster_full: ADOPT', v.t. To take a stranger into one's family as a son; to receive as one's own.
ESSEN'TIAL, a. Necessary to the existence of a thing; important in the highest degree.
SCRU'PLE, n. Doubt; hesitation from the difficulty of determining what is right.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
corruption_summary: The 1729 act by which American Presbyterians adopted Westminster, with the scruple clause.
corruption_paragraphs: The Adopting Act is quoted by every party in every American Presbyterian subscription dispute, and usually by halves. Those who want latitude cite the scruple clause; those who want strictness cite the requirement to subscribe. The act says both, and the question it left unanswered — who decides what is essential and necessary — is the question that has done the dividing.

The principle to recover is that the synod faced the real difficulty rather than evading it. A church must “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) and must have elders able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9); and it must also walk together with men who agree (Amo 3:3) without pretending to an agreement finer than exists.
roots_summary: Greek hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern; hugiaino (G5198), to be sound; Hebrew ya'ad (H3259), to agree.
roots_lines: Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, form, pattern; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy; Titus 1:9.
Hebrew ya'ad (H3259) — to agree, meet by appointment; Amos 3:3.
usage: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — the subscription required.
“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — the scruple clause.
“that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — what the act hoped to secure.

pos: n. (John Thomson, c. 1690–1753, Ulster-born Presbyterian minister, author of the 1727 overture for subscription)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Thomson, son of Thomas.
biblical_def: John Thomson was an Ulsterman, licensed in Ireland and settled in America from 1715, minister at Lewes in Delaware and afterwards in Pennsylvania and Virginia. In 1727 he laid before the Synod of Philadelphia the overture that became the Adopting Act: that the synod require every minister and candidate to subscribe the Westminster Confession and Catechisms, and depose any who taught contrary to them. He had watched the Ulster subscription controversy at first hand and knew where non-subscription led — the Presbytery of Antrim had seceded the year before, and the Arian decay of the Irish synod was already visible. He was opposed by Jonathan Dickinson, who feared a human test over conscience, and the act of 1729 was the compromise between them. Thomson later led the Old Side against the New Side revivalists, published against the itinerancy, and ended his ministry in Virginia. His argument was the one experience had taught the Irish: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an overture as a proposal, something offered for consideration, and to subscribe as to attest by writing one's name beneath.
webster_full: O'VERTURE, n. A proposal; something offered for consideration or acceptance.
SUBSCRI'BE, v.t. To attest by writing one's name beneath; to assent to.
DEPO'SE, v.t. To divest of office; to deprive of an office or dignity.
scriptures: Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: The Ulsterman whose 1727 overture produced the Adopting Act.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Thomson is worth naming because the American subscription debate is usually told as a purely colonial argument about liberty, when the man who forced it was an Ulsterman who had just watched the same argument lose in Ireland. He was not theorising. He had seen presbyteries licensed men who would not say whether Christ is God.

The principle to recover is that contending for the faith is a duty laid on the church corporately and therefore requires some instrument (Jude 1:3). A court that meets to consider the matter (Act 15:6) must have something to consider it by; and a people told to obey those who have the rule over them (Heb 13:17) are entitled to know what those men hold.
roots_summary: Greek epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly; hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern; hegeomai (G2233), to rule.
roots_lines: Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to contend earnestly for; Jude 3.
Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; Jude 3.
Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, have the rule; Hebrews 13:17.
Greek agrupneo (G69) — to watch, keep awake; Hebrews 13:17.
usage: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3) — the overture of 1727.
“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — what Ulster had let go.
“they watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17) — why a congregation may ask.

pos: n. (Peter Williams, 1723–1796, Welsh Methodist hymnwriter and annotator of the Welsh Bible)
etymology: Greek Petros, a rock; Welsh Williams, son of William.
biblical_def: Peter Williams of Llandyfaelog was converted under Whitefield at Carmarthen, served briefly as a curate and was driven out of the established church for Methodist preaching, and became one of the chief itinerants of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist movement alongside Rowland and Harris. His lasting work was the annotated Welsh Bible of 1770, the first Bible with commentary printed in Wales: he revised the text of the 1588 Morgan Bible lightly, added marginal notes and a running exposition, and it went through many editions and was for a century the family Bible of Welsh households and the chief theological education most of them received. He is also the translator and reviser who gave the English-speaking world the hymn Guide me, O thou great Jehovah from William Williams's Welsh. In 1791 the Methodist association excluded him on a charge of Sabellian error in a note on the Trinity, a judgment later generations have thought harsh. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16) describes what his Bible did in Wales.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an annotation as a note added by way of explanation, and a hymn as a song of adoration to God.
webster_full: AN'NOTATION, n. A note, added by way of explanation or comment.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God; among pagans, a poem in honor of a deity.
ITIN'ERANT, a. Passing or travelling about the country; not settled.
scriptures: Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
Psa 96:1
O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth.
corruption_summary: The Welsh itinerant whose annotated Bible of 1770 taught a nation its theology.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The exclusion of Williams in 1791 over a Trinitarian note raises a question churches still face: how to deal with an ageing and much-used servant whose late writing is loose at a point that matters. The association chose discipline over indulgence, at the cost of a reputation; whether it chose rightly is still argued in Wales.

The principle to recover is the end his Bible served: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16). Notes exist to give the sense and cause the people to understand the reading (Neh 8:8); the annotator prays for himself first — “Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law” (Psa 119:18) — because a note carries the authority of the page it sits on.
roots_summary: Greek enoikeo (G1774), to dwell in; plousios (G4146), richly; Hebrew galah (H1540), to uncover.
roots_lines: Greek enoikeo (G1774) — to dwell in, inhabit; Colossians 3:16.
usage: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16) — the Welsh Bible of 1770.
“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — the first annotated Bible in Wales.
“O sing unto the LORD a new song” (Psa 96:1) — and the hymns he carried into English.

pos: n. (Lewis Edwards, 1809–1887, principal of Bala College, the chief theologian of Welsh Calvinistic Methodism)
etymology: Old German Hludwig, famous warrior, whence Lewis; Welsh Edwards, son of Edward.
biblical_def: Lewis Edwards was born at Pwllcenawon in Cardiganshire, kept a school, and in his late twenties went to Edinburgh, where he took a degree and sat under Chalmers; he returned in 1837 to found with his father-in-law David Charles the school at Bala that became the Calvinistic Methodist theological college, and he was its principal for fifty years. He trained most of the ministers of his denomination in two generations, insisting on Greek, Hebrew, logic and philosophy against a strong party which held that a Welsh preacher needed only the Bible and the Spirit. He wrote the standard Welsh works on the atonement and on the doctrine of God, founded and edited Y Traethodydd, the first serious Welsh quarterly, and translated and expounded the Reformed tradition for a people whose theology had been carried almost entirely in sermons and hymns. His argument for the college was 2 Timothy: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a college as a society of men set apart for learning, and theology as divinity, the science of God and divine things.
webster_full: COL'LEGE, n. A society of men set apart for learning or religion; the edifice appropriated to their use.
THEOL'OGY, n. Divinity; the science of God and divine things.
PRIN'CIPAL, n. The head of a college or school; a chief or head.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Bala's principal for fifty years, who gave Welsh Methodism a trained ministry.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Edwards had to fight, within a revival tradition, the conviction that learning cools a preacher — that the great Welsh pulpit of the previous century had been built by men without Greek and that a college would produce lecturers instead of evangelists. He granted the history and denied the inference: those men had been formed by a saturation in Scripture that his own generation no longer had, and the college was how to supply it.

The principle to recover is that the handing on of doctrine requires competence as well as conviction: an elder must be able “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9), and “the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7). Instruction given to a wise man makes him wiser (Pro 9:9); it does not cool him.

“able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — why Greek and Hebrew.
“Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9) — against the party of plain preaching.

pos: n. (John Glas, 1695–1773, minister of Tealing, deposed in 1728, founder of the Glasites)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Gaelic glas, grey or green.
biblical_def: John Glas was minister of Tealing in Angus from 1719, and came by his own study of the New Testament to a conclusion that cost him his place: that the national covenants were unwarranted, that the civil magistrate has no authority in the church at all, and that Christ's kingdom is spiritual and therefore cannot be established by law. In a country whose Reformed identity rested on the Covenants this was intolerable, and after four years of process he was deposed by the Assembly in 1728. He gathered a congregation at Dundee on New Testament lines, and with his son-in-law Robert Sandeman the movement spread to England and to New England as the Glasites or Sandemanians; its best-known member was Michael Faraday. Their worship was austerely literal — weekly communion, the love feast, the kiss of charity, foot-washing, plurality of elders — and Sandeman's doctrine that faith is bare assent to the testimony became a byword for a real error. Glas's own central claim was sound: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines establishment as the settling of a religion by law, and a magistrate as a public civil officer invested with authority.
webster_full: ESTAB'LISHMENT, n. The settling or fixing of a religion by law; the church established by law.
MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of a state.
COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons.
scriptures: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Tealing's minister, deposed in 1728 for denying the magistrate's authority in the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Glas is a double lesson. His central contention — that the church is not established by statute and the magistrate has no spiritual jurisdiction — is now held by most Reformed Christians in the English-speaking world, including those who would have deposed him; he was a century and a half early. But the movement he founded ran to the opposite error through Sandeman, whose definition of faith as bare intellectual assent to the apostolic testimony empties it of trust and of the heart.

The principle to recover is the one Glas had right and paid for: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36), and the things of Caesar and of God are not the same things (Mat 22:21). The church's weapons “are not carnal, but mighty through God” (2Co 10:4), which is why a kingdom that needs a statute to stand is not this one.
roots_summary: Greek basileia (G932), kingdom; apodidomi (G591), to render, give back; sarkikos (G4559), carnal.
roots_lines: Greek enteuthen (G1782) — from hence, from this source; John 18:36.
Greek apodidomi (G591) — to render, pay back; Matthew 22:21.
usage: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) — the claim that cost him Tealing.
“Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's” (Mat 22:21) — and no more.
“the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) — against a church by statute.
